# `fate` test data

Fixtures and reference goldens for the `fate` toolchain. This directory holds **test data
only** — no code, and nothing here is read by a build.

## Layout

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `fixtures/*.fate` | Fate Script sources fed to the compiler under test (21: 2 real + 17 probes + 2 CLI-contract sources) |
| `golden/<id>.expected` | byte-exact assembly text the reference produced for `<id>.fate` |
| `golden/<id>.diag` | reference exit code, whether it wrote a file, and its reported diagnostics |
| `manifest.json` | per-fixture arguments, expected outcome and parity ruling, plus a separate `cli_contract` table |
| `run_golden.py` | the differential harness: runs `fate compile` per fixture and compares |

## Provenance

* `char_utils.fate`, `queen_fury.fate` — copied **verbatim** (no header added) from
  `~/Documents/GitHub/lloyd_mod/patches/libs/`, byte-identical to the copies in
  `~/Documents/GitHub/Severed-Chains/patches/libs/`. These are mod-authored Fate library
  sources from the Severed Chains ecosystem (AGPL-3.0), not retail game data. They are the
  only real-world Fate sources available anywhere: no `.fate` file exists in either reference
  repository's history beyond these two.
* `p*.fate` — synthesized here to probe grammar and diagnostic behaviour. The two-line comment
  header on each is ours. Comments are stripped by the reference lexer, so the header does not
  affect emitted code, but it does shift the line numbers quoted in `.diag`.
* `golden/*` — generated by Script-Recompiler `0.7.11` at `3433e6f74bb6d562aeff0490d11e8937da437511`,
  never hand-written and never edited by hand. The 18 fixtures truncated to a single newline
by a probe script on 2026-10-28 were restored from a same-day copy, and accepted because each
restored source reproduces its `.expected` and `.diag` byte-for-byte — which is what separates
a verified restoration from a plausible-looking guess.

## Regenerating

```
python3 tools/fate_oracle.py build          # copies the reference to scratch and builds it
python3 tools/fate_oracle.py gen            # rewrites golden/ from the reference
python3 tools/fate_oracle.py check          # re-runs and fails on drift (exit 1)
python3 tools/fate_oracle.py status         # what is available / why it would skip
```

Prerequisites, all of which are **optional**: a JDK, Gradle, a local copy of the reference
repository, and a local meta bundle. When any is missing the harness prints `SKIPPED …` and
exits 77 rather than passing silently — the differential harness below uses the same convention.
Nothing here runs during an ordinary **build**; `run_golden.py` does run during an ordinary
**test** pass (next section), which is why it must never invoke Java or the network.

The oracle never builds inside `~/Documents/GitHub/Script-Recompiler`: that tree is read-only
by project rule and is copied into `~/.cache/sc-fate-oracle/src` first.

## Running the differential test

`run_golden.py` is the acceptance harness for `fate compile`. It is registered with CTest as
`fate.compile.golden` (on by default; `-DFATE_ENABLE_GOLDEN_TEST=OFF` opts out), or it can be run
directly:

    cmake -S fate -B build-fate -G Ninja && cmake --build build-fate
    python3 fate/testdata/run_golden.py build-fate/fate fate/testdata

It reads `manifest.json`, runs the built binary once per fixture with that fixture's arguments,
and compares **three axes**: emitted bytes, emitted diagnostics, and exit status. The meta bundle comes from `$FATE_META_DIR`, else from a few local
candidates; if it is absent the run exits **77** with a visible `SKIP:` line and CTest reports
`Skipped` (the test sets `SKIP_RETURN_CODE 77`) rather than `Passed`. A green run in that situation
means "this machine tested nothing", which is why the CI step prints a `NOT VERIFIED` banner
instead of treating it as coverage.

**Two parity modes** (`parity` in `manifest.json`). `match` (18 fixtures) requires byte
equality — that is the default and it applies to every fixture whose source is valid Fate.
`deviation` (`p12_forloop`) is for input that is not valid Fate: the reference's output there is
an ANTLR error-recovery artifact, so the harness instead requires exit status 3, no crash, and
that the output *differs* from the golden — and it reports an obsolete pin if the output ever
matches again, so a stale pin cannot outlive the divergence that justified it.

The `p12` pin is a **test pin, not a claim of semantic equivalence** (owner ruling 2026-10-28,
decision 3). Checking it surfaced that our recovery rule 2 is not local: after the malformed
`for(...)` header the parser consumes the remainder of the function body, so valid statements
following the bad one are dropped. Because that mechanism can destroy valid code, the fixture
stays an open issue; flipping `parity` to `match` in a copy of this directory makes the harness
fail on bytes *and* diagnostics, so the divergence is visible rather than absorbed. The reproducer
and the two candidate fixes are recorded in `docs/research/fate-compile-design.md` §4.2 and §14
item 2.

**Native CLI-contract checks** (`cli_contract` in `manifest.json`). Nine entries, `c1`
through `c9`, in two families. `c1`/`c2` pin `-L` handling: a supplied include directory
that is missing, or is a plain file, stops the run before the program text is discussed.
`c4`/`c5`/`c9` pin the other family — a `def` body calling `helper`, guarded by an `include` of
a file that exists nowhere, which is a fatal compile error rather than a diagnostic to
collect and carry on past. `c9` is the case where that unresolvable include sits *between* two
valid `def`s, so the failure happens after the tool has already parsed real callees: the
contract is that nothing is written, not a half-built program whose call targets are
undefined. `c3` (valid include, exit 0), `c6` (`include char_utils.fate ;`
with the trailing space, which is not a file include at all) and `c7`/`c8` exist so that
the first two families cannot be satisfied by a rule that rejects every include or deletes
every output.

They have no `.expected`/`.diag` pair and are **not** oracle-derived — for both families
the reference does something different on purpose (it aborts with exit 1 on a bad include
directory, and with a stack trace followed by exit 0 on an unresolvable include), so there
is no golden to agree with and ruling R1 does not apply. The harness reports them on their
own line, marked *not derived from the oracle*, so nobody reads them as differential
evidence.

`$MISSING` and `$FIXTURES` expand into a private temporary directory and the fixture
directory respectively. Every entry runs with an explicit `-o` **inside that private
directory**, so these runs cannot write into `fixtures/` or `golden/`; `c8` additionally
compiles a *copy* of a fixture, so the entry that pins "no failing compile may damage its
own source" cannot damage anything but a copy if it ever stops passing.

**Two diagnostic modes** (`diag`). By default a fixture's stderr is compared with the
message lines of `<id>.diag`: order-insensitive (the oracle captured `sorted(set(...))`, so
the artifact carries no emission order) but multiset-strict, so a missing message, an extra
one, or a wrong line prefix fails. The reference's own crash output (`Failed to compile:`
and the `java.*` trace) is filtered from the expectation, because ruling R1 treats it as a
defect and the tool prints nothing like it. `"diag": "unpinned"` (`p12`) switches the
comparison off for a fixture whose difference is a documented recovery by-product — and
prints `NOT VERIFIED` for it, so an unchecked fixture stays visible in the report instead of
passing quietly.

**Inputs are read-only.** Every `fixtures/*.fate`, `golden/*.expected` and `golden/*.diag`
file is hashed before the sweep and re-hashed after it; a run that mutates one of them fails,
naming every changed file. This exists because two probe scripts in this project's history
redirected output onto fixture paths and truncated them while the suite stayed green. The same
rule applies to hand-run probes: always pass `-o` to a path outside this directory.

## Why a meta bundle is part of the recipe

Emitted text contains engine-call names (`call SMap::scriptScaleUniform, …`), which come from
the meta CSVs, so the meta is part of a golden's provenance. Two consequences:

* `snapshot` is deliberately **not** used — the reference always re-fetches `snapshot` from
  `https://legendofdragoon.org/scmeta/`, which would make goldens depend on whatever the server
  returned that day. Any named version reads a local cache directory instead.
* The meta CSVs are **not committed** here. They are reverse-engineering output derived from
  retail script data and stay in a local lane (`~/Documents/GitHub/Severed-Chains/patches/meta`
  by default, overridable with `--meta` or `FATE_ORACLE_META`). `queen_fury.fate` needs
  `legend.game.combat.bent.BattleEntityStat.csv` to exist or the reference throws while loading
  meta; the harness therefore seeds all five CSVs whenever it runs.

## Licensing

The reference is AGPL-3.0. The project owner ruled on 2026-10-27 that **AGPL-derived goldens
may be committed**, which is why `golden/` exists. Hand-written `.txt` disassembly fixtures that
were transcribed from retail script bytes are deliberately **not** imported here — they belong
to a local, opt-in fixture lane — and the two upstream `.fate` sources are committed on the basis
that they are ecosystem-authored source under the same AGPL umbrella, not proprietary assets.
That basis is recorded here so it can be re-checked against the licensing doc rather than
inferred from the presence of the files.

## Reading a golden

Three details are load-bearing and will look like mistakes to a reviewer:

* the file starts with a blank line;
* `return ` carries a trailing space;
* scratch slots are `<function>_expr_<n>` with a double underscore (function name, `_`, then
  `_expr_n`), and both the `_expr_` and `_label_` counters run **per file**, not per function.

`check` compares bytes. Normalising trailing whitespace or line endings would hide real drift,
which is the whole point of the comparison.
